9.10 — Impact, Ethics & Licenses (Your Fork!)

Your whole semester is a FOR: you copied someone else's project, legally, and made it yours. Today: why that was legal, what you owe for it, and the bigger questions — who gets to build games, whose data gets taken, and what happens when "the internet" is where 8 billion people's lives actually live.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Open source and your fork. The starter repo ships a LICENSE file — open yours now (your fork's repo, the file called LICENSE). Read the first line, because it is probably not what you would guess: this project is under the Apache License 2.0, not MIT.

Both are permissive licenses — they let you do almost anything — but Apache 2.0 is the more formal of the two. Here is the phrase from it that does the real work, quoted from section 2 of the file you just opened:

...a perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive, no-charge,
royalty-free, irrevocable copyright license to reproduce,
prepare Derivative Works of, publicly display, publicly
perform, sublicense, and distribute the Work...

That one sentence is why your fork was legal, why you may sell 8.6's build on itch.io, and why nobody can revoke that permission later. In exchange you owe two things: keep the notices, and state that you changed the files. Apache also carries an explicit patent grant that MIT has no clause for at all — a difference that matters enormously to companies. Not all licenses are this permissive:

LicenseYou mayYou must
MITAnything, even commercialKeep the notice
Apache 2.0 (your starter)Anything, even commercialKeep the notice, state your changes, and pass on the patent grant
GPL (copyleft)Use and modify freelyShare YOUR version under GPL too
CC BY / CC BY-SA (assets)Remix art/musicCredit the author; SA = share alike
Proprietary / "all rights reserved"Nothing without permissionAsk first

Attribution is the social contract. Your game uses the starter's code and possibly others' sprites. A CREDITS file is how the chain of gratitude works — and the exam's "impact" questions are exactly this: software is built in communities, licenses are their rules of the road.

Socratic

GPL's copyleft says: fork freely, but your fork must stay open. Apache 2.0 — the license you just read — says: fork freely, close it if you want. Argue ONE side: which produces more good in the world, and why would a company pick Apache while Linux picked GPL? (There is no right answer; there is an argued answer.)

Concept Lab II ~15 min

Digital divide — who is missing from this room. You build games on school machines with fast wifi. The exam's IOC-1 questions ask who is NOT at the table: students without home internet (your 9.7 minimum spec tinker is about access, not just fps), people whose language the tutorials do not speak, the elderly on interfaces designed by 24-year-olds, whole countries whose news feeds run on algorithms they cannot audit. Software scales the designer's assumptions to millions.

Your data and the games you play. Free games monetize attention: they measure session time, churn, and what makes players return (your own 9.5 dataset is that measurement, done honestly and locally — imagine it sent nightly to a server, aggregated across 40 million players, and used to schedule "limited-time" events at YOUR 11pm). The exam calls this targeted and sometimes predatory design. Knowing the pattern is the defense.

Bias with consequences. Connect to 9.6: a hiring algorithm trained on past hires inherits past exclusion; a game tutorial with only one skin tone teaches who it expects. When your jam games reach the showcase (10.1f), your classmates are the users — what assumptions did YOU bake in without noticing? Name one out loud.

Bug Hunt: Ethics scenarios

  1. You find a sprite pack labeled "free sprites" on a random site with no license file. Your showcase is in 3 days. What are your options ranked from legal to risky — and what is the actually-free alternative (Kenney, OpenGameArt, CC0)?
  2. Your jam game posts a "high score" to a server a classmate wrote. What should the PERMISSION screen say, and what did you learn from 9.8 about who can lie to servers?
  3. The exam classic: "A developer's game collects location data to 'improve the experience.' Which concern is most significant?" — write both the answer and the counter-argument developers would give.
  4. You want to sell your semester game on itch.io someday. Your starter is Apache 2.0: what MUST ship with your zip file, and what must you write down about the files you changed? (Read section 4 of the actual LICENSE — it lists your obligations, and one of them surprises people.)
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Ship responsibly

  1. Write your CREDITS file today: starter repo + name its license; every asset you used and its source; your own contribution statement. It belongs in the repo forever.
  2. Write a short README for your fork, with a license sentence for YOUR own work ("code Apache 2.0, art all rights reserved" is a common split — your fork inherits Apache, so keeping it is the easy path). Why do people license code and art differently?
  3. Hard: your showcase audience includes students who cannot play fast-action games (motor, vision). Name ONE accessibility feature from your own semester you could add in a week (rebindable keys? a one-button mode — which you already prototyped for the 2-button jam, 10.1a).

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain permissive vs copyleft vs proprietary, using your fork's own Apache 2.0 license as the evidence
  • Write a correct CREDITS file with sources and licenses
  • Describe the digital divide with two concrete examples
  • Identify one assumption your own design baked in, and one fix
